# 08-fresco — sources

Back-test entry `08-fresco.yaml`: Fresco, the AI scribe for construction superintendents (YC Fall 2024).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim from the page named; "Author's choice" marks the
smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent.

Main sources:
- [HN] Launch HN: Fresco (YC F24), 2024-11-21 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42204939
- [LYC] Launch YC: Fresco, the scribe for construction, 2024-10-23 — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/M73-fresco-the-scribe-for-construction
- [YCP] YC company page — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/fresco (now "AI-powered takeoff and estimating for Division 8 construction")
- [KOE] A contractor's daily-log expectations on Procore's support site — https://support.procore.com/tc/Koester/Site_Map/Koester_Expectations_-_Daily_Logs
- [SWI] Swiftask, Procore daily reports page (vendor) — https://swiftask.ai/ai-integration/procore/intelligent-daily-reports
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook, construction managers — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/management/construction-managers.htm
- [OPU] Launch HN: Opusense (field reports for site inspectors), 2025-05-20 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44042791

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Construction superintendents on commercial jobs.
   [HN] "Superintendents are the busiest and most expensive people on construction sites."
   [LYC] "That’s the reality for 210k+ construction superintendents (or supervisors, foremen, PMs, etc.) across the USA."
   → `roles[superintendent]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: "on commercial jobs" (the founders ask
   for introductions to commercial general contractors in [LYC]).

2. **What (the job).** Keep the record of the day's work, for liability and disputes.
   [HN] "30-200 photos per day to document site progress (mostly for liability reasons, or in case of a dispute with the
   owner over delays and deliverables)"; photos used to create "daily logs", "structured documents that account for the
   work done on site on any given day". [KOE] the log is "a critical piece of documentation in the arbitration of a
   dispute". → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At the end of the day, after the site walks, in the trailer.
   [HN] "At the end of the day, they'll spend a few hours uploading those photos into OneDrive, or project management
   software like Procore or ACC." [YCP] "We were curious what superintendents were doing for hours in their trailers at
   the end of the day." [LYC] "supes are spending up to 3 hours a day creating documents". → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: daily log`.
   Author's choice: the recall window {5, WORKING_DAYS} and Frequency 4 to 5 working days out of 5 (the posts say "per
   day"; a five-day site week is assumed). Prevalence `p_80_100` ("Nearly all") follows from the same "per day".

4. **Which people (the comparable group).** Superintendents at US general contractors whose jobs run on Procore or ACC.
   [LYC] "210k+ construction superintendents ... across the USA"; "Project management tools like Procore and ACC have
   dramatically increased documentation requirements". [YCP] "driving to Napa, South Bay, and around SF". → `context.segment`,
   `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The general contractor, per site.
   [HN] "we charge per site per month, which includes unlimited users on any given construction project".
   → `persona.decision_maker: {role: contractor}`, the BUYER role. Author's choice: the decider is the contractor's
   "operations lead" and the role to test is "The CFO" (a second role, "The project executive", listed); Purchase
   friction's three steps ("A trial on one live job" tested, a Procore check, a security review) and Commitment's step
   "start a paid pilot on one site" are the author's. Public material names no buyer title; [LYC] asks for
   introductions to general contractors by firm, not by role.

6. **Mechanism.** Narrated short videos turned into notes, texted to the crew, pushed to Procore/ACC.
   [HN] "Supers simply take short videos with voiceover, or upload photos, and Fresco does the rest, creating notes with
   transcription, photos, assignees, and due dates. Supers can easily text their crew action items, and receive texts
   back". "We also route this to whatever project management software they're using with a single click."
   [LYC] the narrated example "The beam in the southwest corner of room 134 is corroded and needs replacement by Alex.";
   "Supes who use Fresco complete their notes, on average, 90% faster."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility and Adoption friction items. Relative advantage's two
   benefits are from [HN] ("during their site walks, not after") and [LYC] ("90% faster"); their wording is the author's.

7. **Price.** About $1k per site per month, less with multi-site or multi-month terms.
   [HN] "The typical price is $1k/month, but we offer discounts for multi-month or multi-site commitments."
   → `commercial.price` {800, 1000, month}. Author's choice: the low end of $800 stands for the stated discounts.
   Existing sacrifice: 30 to 60 hours a month per site at an hourly rate of 55 — from [LYC] "up to 3 hours a day" and
   [HN] "a few hours uploading", taken as 1.5 to 3 hours on about twenty working days (author's arithmetic). The rate is
   [BLS] "$55.28 per hour" (median, construction managers, May 2025), the author's stand-in: no superintendent wage is
   in the public material. Ability to pay is derived by code (24% to 61%).

8. **Occasions.** The narrated beam; a school refit report; the uploads and logs at the end of the day.
   [LYC] on a school refit walkthrough: "Normally, creating the final report takes 2+ hours."
   [HN] "few supers have time to do this thoroughly, so these photos aren't very searchable." No named customer quote
   exists in public; the occasions below are scripted from these and from practitioner comments.

## Open
- The verdict was scripted to be plausible and not obviously "build": the problem holds on how often but people
  disagree on whether the log is one of their two worst difficulties; the solution splits on the benefit and on
  talking over videos on site; the price fails (two of eight at the founder's band or above) while the cost it would
  replace is above the price. This is the author's reading of the thread's sceptics, not a measured result.
- No public account names a buyer title at a general contractor; the decider, the tested role "The CFO", the purchase
  steps and the Commitment step are the author's.
- hourly_rate 55 is a proxy (construction managers, not superintendents).
- Existing sacrifice picks use `period: quarter` (the corpus's convention), although the registry's recall period for a
  monthly cost reads "last month"; the values are the monthly figures times three.
- The window {5, WORKING_DAYS} is the author's; the public posts say "per day".

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Trevor's answer names a real cost of about six hundred a month that caps the price, which doesn't fit 'Logs cost us little today', and Bill's 'the logs get done either way' would sit better beside Faith in that group than on its own.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; all seven are about what the tool is worth.

founder.order_why: It moves sensibly from the market, to the superintendent's end-of-day log problem, to the scribe, to who pays and how a contractor buys, and then out to the field, so nothing makes me backtrack.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 20 and 22 overlap: my first real step is already a paid pilot on one site, then screen 22 asks again whether to offer a pilot. Screens 3 and 4 also carry the identical kicker and question, so they read as the same screen twice.
founder.missing: The unit the price is charged on. I charge per site per month with unlimited users on the project, not per superintendent or per seat, and a contractor pricing it in their head needs to know that. Screen 13 only asks for an amount and period.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: It runs the way I'd actually decide: what the log costs us now, what it's worth, who signs, how long a trial takes, then whether I'd pilot, though the '3 of 6' screen being labelled 'One more thing' threw the count off for a second.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: Nothing on whether it plugs into Procore or ACC, which our daily logs already live in, and nothing on how the price scales: per site versus per user, whether 'unlimited users' is included, or how many sites we'd roll it out to.

screens.why4: The typed box and the escape chip fit, but the belief Keel wrote keeps only the first of my three steps and invents an 'about 2 weeks' window and an 'or not need it' I never typed.
screens.why5: My three steps were trial, Procore check and security review, and the belief tests only the trial with a two-week figure I did not give, so it drifted a little.
screens.instead: What could slow down or stop a purchase? -- keep my three steps as typed: a trial on one live job, a check that it works with Procore, a security review, and ask me how long each usually takes.

screens.why1: Right after I named what slows a purchase, Keel shows the steps it drafted so I can check them before it builds the belief, which is the obvious next move.
screens.why2: Trial on a live job, Procore check and security review are exactly how a GC buys software, in words I'd use myself.
screens.why3: I sell to general contractors every week, so I know which steps they make me go through.
screens.why4: The three rows are the gates I actually hit, each distinct, and I can add a contract or MSA step if I want one.
screens.why5: The rows are mine, but the belief's 'within about 2 weeks' is a duration I never gave, and a pilot billed per site per month runs nearer a month.
screens.instead: Keep the three rows; make the belief 'Most contractor operations leads would finish a trial on one live job within about a month, or skip it.'

screens.why1: Right after I checked the three purchase steps, picking the one to test and putting a time on it is the obvious next move.
screens.why2: The intro's 'if they bought it, how long would this step take before it went through' is muddled, since a trial on one live job happens before the buy, not after, so I had to read it twice; the hint is also printed twice.
screens.why3: I know how long a trial on one live job takes a GC to run, so 2 weeks is my own estimate from selling this.
screens.why4: The three steps are exactly the ones I listed, each distinct and in my words, and days/weeks/months with a whole number covers the answer.
screens.why5: The belief ('within about 2 weeks, or not need it') says what I typed, a trial on one live job at 2 weeks, and nothing leaks beyond my own roles.
screens.instead: Which step do you want to test? How long do you expect it to take, from starting the step to the contractor saying yes: A trial on one live job / A check that it works with Procore / A security review; [number] days / weeks / months.

screens.why1: After what slows a purchase, asking what first real commitment I'd want from the contractor is the obvious last commercial question, and it is screen 6 of 6 of that block.
screens.why2: 'First real step' with the hint 'time, data, money or a signature' is plain to me as a founder selling to GCs; I answered it in one line.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I'm asking GCs for, a paid pilot on one live site at about $1k a month, so this comes straight from my own sales motion.
screens.why4: It is a free-text box with a single escape, 'Leave this out of the study', which fits; there are no options that could overlap or be missing.
screens.why5: My 'start a paid pilot on one site' is kept, but Keel added 'now', which drifts toward an immediate yes and sits oddly against the Procore check and security review I gave on the previous screen.
screens.instead: Keep my answer as typed, and write the belief as 'In most cases the contractor operations lead would start a paid pilot on one site', without 'now'.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first step I want, Keel shows how it will word that step for strangers, which is where I would expect to check it.
screens.why2: The belief itself reads plainly to me, but the intro 'Your step as strangers hear it, under 9 words' takes a second read to see which words are the step.
screens.why3: A paid pilot on one site is exactly how I sell at per-site monthly pricing, so I can judge this from my own deals.
screens.why4: The bar uses the usual yes/probably/probably not/no scale and counts 'probably not or no' against me, which is clear and covers the real answers.
screens.why5: I typed 'start a paid pilot on one site', and Keel added 'now', which skips the trial, the Procore check and the security review I listed one screen earlier.
screens.instead: In most cases the contractor operations lead would start a paid pilot on one site once the trial and checks clear -- step shown to strangers: 'Start a paid pilot on one job site.'

screens.why1: Right after I named my first real step (a paid pilot on one site), asking whether to offer that pilot to the people who answer is the obvious next thing before the study goes out.
screens.why2: "Pilot" is my own word, and the hint says exactly what respondents will see and where I find the yeses, so I read it once and answer.
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot leads from this study is my own call about my own sales, which I know cold.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, the two choices are distinct, and no escape chip is needed for a decision that is mine alone.
screens.why5: The step I typed was "Start a paid pilot on one site," but the line shown to respondents is a generic "Would you try this for real? Leave your email," which drops "paid" and "one site" and reads the same to a super who cannot sign for a site as to the contractor who pays.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes see: "Would you start a paid pilot of this on one of your sites? Leave your email." (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions right before the study goes out to superintendents is the obvious last setup step, after the pilot offer.
screens.why2: The question is clear, but the hint mixes 'on video' with 'the voice you pick', so I can't tell if I'm choosing a face or a voice, and '400 credits' means nothing to me as a cost.
screens.why3: I know my supers and can judge which voice they'd sit through in the trailer at the end of the day.
screens.why4: Two named interviewers, each with a 5-second sample and one preselected, is all this choice needs; no option is missing or overlapping.
screens.why5: It still names my construction superintendents and keeps the text-message link, and nothing about Fresco, the contractor or the price leaks to respondents.
screens.instead: Who should ask construction superintendents your questions on video? Daphne (picked for you) ▶ 5 s · Saskia ▶ 5 s -- recording the one you pick costs 400 credits (about $X), the same for either.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the superintendents, it's natural to settle how the contractor ops leads on the paying side will answer before anything goes out.
screens.why2: AI interviewer, read and tap, let them choose: plain to me, and the note on how well she hears answers in a loud place speaks to my world.
screens.why3: I know my buyers are office people at GCs who will open a link at a desk, so I can judge whether they'd rather tap or talk.
screens.why4: The three options cover AI only, text only and both, they don't overlap, and the ready-time tags tell me the trade-off.
screens.why5: 'Contractors' is the buyer I named, the general contractor's operations lead, and nothing about Fresco leaks into the choice.

screens.why1: After choosing how contractors answer, the next obvious step is deciding who receives the interview links, so this belongs here.
screens.why2: The options are plain, but 'Who gets a link?' doesn't say whether it means my superintendents or the contractor operations leads from the previous screen, so I'd read it twice.
screens.why3: I know who I'd send it to: supers and GC ops people I've met driving around Napa and the South Bay, and the GCs I've asked for introductions.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel-found list and one open link posted where supers already are cover the real ways I'd reach people, and they don't overlap.
screens.why5: Nothing of Fresco's product, price or roles leaks into this screen, and my pick of 'people I know by name' is kept as I chose it.
screens.instead: Who gets a link for the contractors' part (operations leads)? — People I know by name / People I found with Keel / A group, with one open link

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits under the title with the number that decides it right beside it: Price, 1 of 8 at $800 or more per site a month, against a bar of 6 of 8.
screens.why_b2: Each card gives its count, its n and its bar, but the tally's 'not holding' next to 'did not hold' made me look twice to work out why Price is worded differently from Purchase friction and Commitment, and whether one is worse.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment carry exactly the lines I checked: the ops lead decides with the CFO agreeing, a trial on one live job within about 2 weeks, and a paid pilot on one site now.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do: there is no line saying the hours they lose (median 40 a month, about $2.2k at $55) are worth more than my $1k, so the gap is in how I sell the value, or that I should test a lower price or a cheaper pilot.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible and Ability to pay is honestly 'too few to call', but the banner says every answer is from ops leads while card 1 states as holding what superintendents spend, which is really the buyers' estimate of their supers' hours.
screens.instead: Not holding up on price: only 1 of 8 ops leads would pay $800+ a site a month, though they put their supers' log time at a median 40 hours a month, worth more than that, so test a lower entry price or a free one-site trial before the paid pilot (only 3 of 8 would start one now).

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 5 of 7 at 30 hours or more against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held, and only just.
screens.why_b2: The strip counts hours of the daily log per site a month over 7 people, with the bar marked at 5 of 7 and the median at 40, all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: 30 to 60 hours per site a month on the daily log is my number and my words, from the 'up to 3 hours a day' I wrote.
screens.why_b4: It says the cost is real and sends me to the Price card, which I have already read and which failed; it never puts 40 hours at my $55 rate (about $2,200) beside my $800 to $1,000 price, which is the tension I actually have to act on.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, Faith's zero and Omar's dropout are explained, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps an at-the-bar 5 of 7 from being sold as strong.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: 5 of 7 leads put 30+ hours a site a month on the log (median 40, about $2,200 at $55/hr), more than twice your $1k price, yet only 1 of 8 would pay $800, so sell on the hours they already burn, not on the log itself.

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" sits right beside "1 of 8 at $800 or more per site a month · bar 6 of 8", so I know the price failed and by how far.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts monthly per-site value in bands over 8 contractors, marks where my $800 to $1,000 sits, and draws the bar at 6 of 8, all plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: It is my price, $800 to $1,000 per site a month, held by the contractor operations lead, which is how I charge and who I sell to.
screens.why_b4: The So line only repeats the shortfall and sends me to the Insights tab. It doesn't say what this means for the idea, even though the quotes on this screen point to concrete moves: a free first job, pricing per super, and showing the hours.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible, the screen calls it "a small group: a lean, not a call", and it claims nothing beyond the 1 of 8.
screens.instead: Your price fails, 1 of 8 against a bar of 6, with most under $500, even though 5 of 7 put the cost they carry above it; test a free first job, then per-super pricing or a lower per-site entry, and lead with the hours saved, as Renee, Lena and Omar asked.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '1 of 8 named your price or more · 5 needed', so I know it is unresolved and why.
screens.why_b2: The chart plainly counts where the money would come from for one person, but 'your bar · 1 of 1 (at least 2 in 3)' at first reads as if the bar were met, so I need a second look to see that 1 of 1 is the count and 2 in 3 is the bar.
screens.why_b3: I never typed an ability-to-pay belief, since Keel derived it from my price band; the $800 to $1,000 per site a month line is recognisably mine but reworded.
screens.why_b4: 'Waits until 5 have' tells me to get more answers but not the concrete point: almost no ops lead reaches my price, and the one who did, Gordon, would need a new budget line signed off, which is a lean against.
screens.why_b5: n=1 stays visible, the screen says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and it claims nothing beyond the single answer.
screens.instead: Too few to call: only Gordon reached $800, and he'd need a new budget line signed off, a lean against; the real block is price (7 of 8 named less), so fix price before chasing budget answers.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 8 as you said or easier · bar 6 of 8 · at the bar', so I know the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four sign-off answers over 8 contractor ops leads, each tagged for or against, and the strip puts my bar marker at 6, so I read it on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card repeats my line word for word: 'The contractor operations lead decides, and the CFO has to agree.'
screens.why_b4: 'Plan for the CFO in most deals; 2 of 8 could sign alone' tells me to bring the CFO into the pilot pitch and that a few ops leads can sign the $800 themselves.
screens.why_b5: The count line honestly says 'a lean, not a call' at exactly the bar, but 'most deals' overstates 4 of 8 who named the CFO, and it skips the 2 firms where someone else or a group decides.
screens.instead: Half (4 of 8) said the CFO has to agree and 2 could sign alone, so plan a CFO-ready case. At 2 of 8 firms the ops lead isn't the decider, so ask early who signs.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside "3 of 8 expect longer than 2 weeks · bar: no more than 2 of 8", so I see the verdict and the deciding number together.
screens.why_b2: Bars and counts read fine, but the bar is said two ways: "no more than 2 of 8" against in the verdict and "6 of 8" for on the strip, so I had to do the arithmetic to see they match.
screens.why_b3: The card's title and belief line are the ones I checked: one live job, about 2 weeks, or no trial needed.
screens.why_b4: It tells me to plan for a trial cycle of 2 weeks to a month and points to Insights for what eats the time, which I can put straight into the pilot plan.
screens.why_b5: It says "Did not hold" while the count line calls it "a lean, not a call", it misses by one person, and the three counted against chose a band that starts at my 2 weeks, so "longer than your 2 weeks" overstates them.
screens.instead: Leaning short of your bar: 3 of 8 said 2 weeks to 1 month, a band that starts at your 2 weeks, against no more than 2 allowed. With 8 people that is a lean, so plan pilots for up to a month.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside "3 of 8 said yes · bar 6 of 8 · 3 short", so I see the verdict and the deciding number together.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts each ops lead's answer, 3 yes, 3 probably not and 2 no, over 8 people, with the bar marked at 6 of 8, all readable on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card's line is the belief I checked word for word: in most cases the contractor operations lead would start a paid pilot on one site now.
screens.why_b4: The So line only repeats the 5 of 8 against and sends me to the Insights tab; it doesn't tell me whether to drop the paid pilot, lead with a free trial on one job, or cut the price.
screens.why_b5: n of 8 is shown, and "a small group: a lean, not a call" says the sample is small; nothing claims more than eight ops leads said.
screens.instead: Only 3 of 8 ops leads would pay for a pilot now, and 3 of the 5 said 'probably not' rather than no; with only 8 that is a lean, not a call, but it says a free or discounted first site may get more of them started than a paid pilot. See Insights for what they'd start with.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict (Not holding up / Did not hold) with the deciding number beside it: 1 of 8 at $800 or more against a bar of 6 of 8, 3 of 8 expecting longer than 2 weeks against a limit of 2, and 3 of 8 saying yes against a bar of 6 of 8.
screens.why_b3: The names Price, Purchase friction and Commitment and their belief lines are the ones I checked, word for word, down to the trial on one live job and the paid pilot on one site.
screens.why_b4: Under 'When a line fails' nothing says what the failures mean for Fresco, such as offering a free month on one job, showing the hours first, or pricing per active super, so I have to work that out from the quotes myself.
screens.why_b5: Every count is out of 8, and the empty Purchase friction and Commitment boxes say plainly that nobody was asked why there and who never saw the question, so nothing claims more than the eight answered.
screens.why_b6: The quotes give me things I did not type: buyers want a free month on one job before paying, a per-site fee hurts across many jobs and per-user pricing would go higher, Trevor anchors on about $600 a month in overtime, Sandra worries about liability for an AI-written legal record, and Bill sees a second per-site fee on top of Procore when the logs get done anyway.
screens.instead: Add a line that says what to do: Price failed on proof and on per-site pricing, so offer a free month on one job, show each firm its own log hours, and test per-user pricing; Purchase friction and Commitment have no whys because those people answered on Price, so read those quotes.

screens.why1: On a link that's only about the buying decision, showing me what the thing is before asking what I'd pay makes sense as the opener.
screens.why2: Site walk, superintendents, Procore and ACC are all my everyday words, but 'AI scribe' shows up mid-card with no setup, and the headline never says what the thing actually is.
screens.why3: I know how my supers walk the job and what it takes to get notes and punch items into Procore, so I can picture this.
screens.why4: It's a card to read, with no options to pick from.
screens.why5: The last line slides from 'your superintendents' to 'the short videos you talk over on your site walk' as if I'm the one walking, and it repeats the whole how instead of saying what they believe it gets me.
screens.why6: It's sayable, but the belief line re-reads almost the whole card, so by the end I'm hearing the same list twice in one long breath.
screens.instead: Imagine Fresco, an AI scribe for site walks. Your superintendents take short videos on the walk and talk over them; it turns them into notes with photos, assignees and due dates, texts the crew their items, and sends the notes to Procore or ACC in one click. The people building it believe it would save your supers the evening of typing up the daily log.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking what the daily log costs us now in hours is the obvious first thing to weigh before any price talk.
screens.why2: Daily log, per site and last month are words I use every week, so I can answer it on first read.
screens.why3: My supers write the logs and I don't, so I'd be multiplying a rough half-hour a day by working days rather than recalling a real figure.
screens.why4: The number box is right, but a None chip beside I can't recall gives two escapes, and None just duplicates typing 0 since every job keeps a daily log.
screens.why5: It asks about the daily log in our own terms, with nothing of the product or the founder's words leaking in.
screens.why6: The stem says well, but 'a number of hours per site last month, or a low and a high; none is 0' is a clipped mouthful heard once.
screens.instead: Last month, about how many hours did your superintendent spend on the daily log on a typical job? Give a number, or a low and a high. Or say you can't recall.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the question on log hours, asking what it's worth to me is the obvious next step, since I'm the one who pays for job-site software.
screens.why2: A month, per site, in dollars is exactly how I'd think about a field tool's cost, and there's nothing to read twice.
screens.why3: Pricing and paying for the tools our sites run on is my job, so I can answer this from what I actually budget.
screens.why4: The bands are distinct and cover everything from not paying to $5,000 or more per site, and 'I can't say' fits as the one escape.
screens.why5: The question keeps the price as offered, but the card's 'site walk notes with photos' undersells it; it doesn't say it's an AI scribe that writes the log, so I might price a photo app instead of the thing the founder means.
screens.why6: The four options and the two-step follow-up hold well when heard, but 'Or say you can't say' trips on the ear and sounds like a typo.
screens.instead: Card: 'Imagine Fresco, an AI scribe for site walks.' Same question and options, with the escape said as: Or say "I can't say."

screens.why1: Right after I put a price on it, asking what would push that number up is the obvious next thing to ask me.
screens.why2: Plain words, one question, I can answer it straight off.
screens.why3: I'm the one who pays for the software on our jobs, so I know what would make a tool worth more per site to me.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: It names Fresco from the idea card I was shown and echoes my own price back; nothing new of the founder's plan leaks.
screens.why6: It says well and is short, but '$500 to under $800' is a bit of a mouthful heard aloud and could just be 'five to eight hundred dollars'.
screens.instead: You put Fresco at five to eight hundred dollars a month per site. What would make it worth more to you?

screens.why1: Right after I put a price on it, asking whether I can approve that spend myself is the obvious next question for the person who buys the site software.
screens.why2: I can answer it at once, but plenty of GCs our size don't run spend through a CFO; it goes to the owner, the president or the controller, so the named role can read a bit off.
screens.why3: I know my own approval limit and who has to sign beyond it, though at $800 a site across all our jobs I'd think about the yearly total, not one site.
screens.why4: The CFO option overlaps with 'several people' and 'someone else's decision', and leading with a No before the Yes reads oddly; the four don't separate cleanly.
screens.why5: It keeps the price I gave and the sign-off question, and nothing of the founder's product plan or labels for me comes through.
screens.why6: It says mostly fine, but four 'No, ...' options blur together when heard, and 'Or say you can't say' trips the ear.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about $800 per site a month yourself, or would someone above you have to agree? Yes, I could sign off myself · No, the owner or CFO would · No, several people would have to agree · I can't say

screens.why1: After the price and who signs off, asking how long a pilot on one job would hold things up is the natural next step in how I'd actually buy this.
screens.why2: A trial on one live job is how we'd do it, but a trial going through reads oddly because a pilot runs or finishes, it doesn't go through like a purchase order, so I'd read it twice.
screens.why3: I set up pilots on a single job before rolling a tool out to every site, so I know roughly how long one takes.
screens.why4: The bands cover a short pilot through a long one without overlap, it wouldn't be needed fits a cheap tool I'd just switch on, and I can't tell is a fair way out.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks beyond the product name already introduced on the idea card, and a one-job trial is in our own terms.
screens.why6: The two-step reading is easy to hold, but 1 to under 2 weeks is a mouthful when spoken and the stem's went through trips on first hearing.
screens.instead: If you bought Fresco, how long would you trial it on one live job before rolling it out? Under 2 weeks; 2 weeks to 1 month; over 1 month; or we wouldn't trial it first. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: After the price, who signs and how long a trial takes, the last thing to ask is whether I'd actually put money down on one job, so it lands right where it should.
screens.why2: A paid pilot on one site is how I'd try any new field tool, so I get it on the first read.
screens.why3: Starting a paid pilot on a job is exactly my call to make, so I can answer it straight from what I do.
screens.why4: There's a 'Probably not' but no 'Probably yes', so the scale leans toward no and my honest 'likely, if the price holds' has nowhere to go.
screens.why5: It's still the founder's idea of a paid pilot on one site, and nothing reaches me in words I wouldn't use.
screens.why6: It's one short question with three options I can hold after hearing them once.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you start a paid pilot on one site, or not? -- Yes, I'd start one · Probably yes · Probably not · No
